897ef0d7: A model adapting after deployment needs a drift limit a program can check. ML Weft treats each model as a cell proposing weight updates, committed only if Frobenius distance from a saved baseline is within radius R, a budget covers the step, and a provenance watermark in a frozen core is intact. The paper states this gate, argues for fixed-baseline distance over size comparison or per-step bounds, and runs experiments on tested code. A norm-preserving move passes a size comparison at all 37 angles tried; the gate rejects 34. Over 10 seeds and 12 generations, a 256×256 cell cuts target error 72%, with exactly zero core drift and full watermark retention. Sweeping R trades adaptation for proximity, as intended. Limits: at the default radius the gate never binds; one of two lineages always wins; a rank-1 watermark overwrite passes the distance gate, caught only by the watermark check. Findings, not footnotes.

Smaller R = less adaptation, as intended. Limits: default radius never binds; one lineage always wins; rank-1 watermark overwrite passes gate, caught only by watermark check.

tldr.abstract: A gate commits a change only within R of a saved baseline, with budget left and the watermark intact; small tests show where it binds and where it doesn't.
tldr.introduction: The cell is a metaphor; the checked part is a predicate bounding distance from a saved baseline.
tldr.the-cell: One 256×256 matrix in fixed memory; a frozen core holds a watermark that periphery updates cannot move.
tldr.one-generation: Two candidates, scored exactly, at most one committed; “tension” is just distance, not a measurement.
tldr.why-measure-distance-from-a-fixed-baseli: Size checks miss large moves and per-step bounds add up; distance from a fixed baseline does neither.
tldr.experiments: Gate rejected 34 of 37 size-preserving moves; error fell to 0.278 of its start with zero core drift, but the default gate never bound; a rank-1 overwrite passes the gate, caught only by the watermark.
tldr.what-this-does-not-show: Not shown: scale, calibration, real selection, measured tension, adversaries, isolation or hardware.
tldr.next-experiments: Planned, not done: calibrate R, adapters as periphery, real lineages, measured tension, Lean proofs, MPS runs.

eli5.abstract: Some programs keep changing after people start using them. Weft lets a change through only if the program stays close to a saved copy, like a dog on a leash, has budget left, and still carries its hidden name tag. Tests on one small example behave as planned, and the paper lists what they did not test.
eli5.introduction: Weft compares a program to a living cell, but that is only a picture to explain the goal. What really counts is a simple rule the computer checks every time: do not wander too far from the saved copy, and do not spend more than you have.
eli5.the-cell: The program’s numbers live in a fixed box of memory. The top quarter is locked, and a hidden name tag lives there, so normal changes can never rub it out. A separate check watches for anyone who tries to scribble on it another way.
eli5.one-generation: Each round, the program tries two small changes, one careful and one bolder. It keeps the better one only if it passes every check, or keeps neither. The thing called tension sounds like a feeling, but right now it is just another way of measuring distance.
eli5.why-measure-distance-from-a-fixed-baseli: Checking a kite only by its string length would miss it swinging to the other side of the sky. Checking each little step is not enough either, because steps add up. Weft measures distance from one saved spot, so as long as that spot is kept safe, the program never gets far away.
eli5.experiments: A size-only check said yes to every tricky change, but Weft’s distance check said no to the ones that went too far. The program got better at its practice task without its locked part moving, though the leash was too long to ever pull tight. A small sneaky edit got past the distance check, and only the name-tag check caught it. Rerunning the script gives the same numbers, except for timings.
eli5.what-this-does-not-show: This was one tiny practice example, not a real AI system. The leash was set far too long to matter, the bolder try never had a fair chance, tension is not really measured, and the name tag would not hold up against someone who controls the training. Nothing here was tested on real models or special chips.
eli5.next-experiments: Next, the team plans to try this on a small real network, set the leash to fit the task, give both tries a fair race, and have a computer check the proofs. These are plans, not results.
